title: Unitary Designs From Doped Matchgate Circuits
authors: Fabian Ballar Trigueros, Zheng-Hang Sun, Xhek Turkeshi, Piotr Sierant, Poetri Sonya Tarabunga
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matchgate circuits realize free-fermion dynamics: they are efficiently classically simulable, yet cannot on their own generate the generic randomness required for universal computation or unitary design formation. We study a controlled route beyond this integrable limit by doping matchgate circuits with non-Gaussian gates-physically, the injection of fermionic interactions into an otherwise free system. Using the matchgate commutant framework, we obtain analytic control over unitary [MATH]-design formation. For globally scrambled dynamics, the design problem maps exactly onto a classical birth-death Markov chain with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck continuum limit, recasting the emergence of quantum randomness in terms of spectral gaps and mixing times and yielding rigorous bounds on the number of non-Gaussian gates needed for approximate [MATH]-designs. These bounds hold for a broad class of parity-preserving non-Gaussian gates, independently of microscopic details, with numerics indicating that the same mechanism governs higher-order designs. Used as local building blocks in a glued-circuit architecture, they yield approximate parity-preserving [MATH]-designs in polylogarithmic depth with a sparse non-Gaussian gate count, with implications for Page-like entanglement growth and fermionic classical-shadow protocols. Finally, locality reshapes this picture: in local brickwork dynamics, design formation is diffusion-limited and far slower. Our results establish doped matchgate circuits as a controlled, analytically tractable route from free fermions to interaction-generated quantum designs.
tldr: This paper analytically studies how doping matchgate circuits with non-Gaussian gates generates unitary designs, providing rigorous bounds on the number of gates needed.
motivation: Matchgate circuits are classically simulable but cannot generate quantum randomness; understanding how to break this integrability is key to quantum advantage.
method: Using the matchgate commutant framework, the design problem is mapped to a classical birth-death Markov chain with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck limit, yielding spectral gap and mixing time analysis.
result: Rigorous bounds on the number of non-Gaussian gates for approximate t-designs are derived, and a glued-circuit architecture achieves polylogarithmic-depth parity-preserving designs.
conclusion: Doped matchgate circuits provide a controlled, analytically tractable route from free fermions to interaction-generated quantum designs, with implications for entanglement growth and classical shadows.

title: Efficient Graph State Purification With Factorized Graph-Preserving Operations Across Local Clifford Orbits
authors: Mingyuan Wang, Guus Avis, Kenneth Goodenough, Stefan Krastanov
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph states form a broad class of multipartite entangled states underlying measurement-based quantum computation, quantum networks, and stabilizer codes. However, systematic entanglement distillation for arbitrary graph states remains challenging because the circuit design space grows rapidly with the number of parties. We introduce a group of Clifford operations that we call "factorized graph-preserving". It enables us to efficiently enumerate and optimize graph-state purification circuits at finite size for realistic noisy hardware. These operations map products of graph-basis states to products of graph-basis states, so their action can be represented as permutations of graph-basis labels. Moreover, this useful gate set admits a compact factorized description determined by simple graph-theoretic features. This structure also allows, after some initial cached precomputation, drastically lower computational complexity for simulating a gate. We further organize these operations over local-complementation (LC) orbits using minimum-edge representatives (MERs), which let us design purification circuits that apply to all locally equivalent graph states (up to a basis change). Using this framework, we optimize noisy finite-size multipartite distillation circuits for several graph-state families. Numerical results show that the resulting graph-preserving circuits can outperform standard recurrence-based purification protocols under realistic gate and measurement noise. Our results establish LC-orbit structure and factorized graph-preserving operations as practical tools for scalable, topology-aware and hardware-constrained graph-state distillation protocol design. Our work can also be interpreted as a graph-based heuristic for finding transversal gates.
tldr: Introduces factorized graph-preserving Clifford operations to efficiently design and optimize graph-state purification circuits for noisy quantum networks.
motivation: Systematic entanglement distillation for arbitrary graph states is challenging due to the large circuit design space; existing methods are not scalable or hardware-aware.
method: Defines factorized graph-preserving operations that act as permutations on graph-basis labels, enabling efficient enumeration and optimization. Uses local-complementation orbits and minimum-edge representatives to generalize purification circuits across locally equivalent graph states.
result: Numerical results show that the optimized circuits outperform standard recurrence-based purification protocols under realistic gate and measurement noise.
conclusion: The framework provides scalable, topology-aware tools for designing graph-state distillation protocols, with potential applications in quantum networks and measurement-based quantum computing.

The paper further organizes these operations over local-complementation (LC) orbits using minimum-edge representatives (MERs), allowing circuits to apply to all locally equivalent graph states up to a basis change. Using this framework, the authors optimize noisy finite-size multipartite distillation circuits for several graph-state families, demonstrating that FGP circuits can outperform standard recurrence-based purification protocols under realistic gate and measurement noise. The work establishes LC-orbit structure and FGP operations as practical tools for scalable, topology-aware, and hardware-constrained graph-state distillation protocol design, and can be interpreted as a graph-based heuristic for finding transversal gates.

Development of a compact factorized description for FGP gates based on simple graph-theoretic features, reducing computational complexity for simulation.
Organization of FGP operations over local-complementation (LC) orbits using minimum-edge representatives (MERs) to design circuits applicable to all locally equivalent graph states.
Numerical demonstration that FGP-based distillation circuits outperform standard recurrence-based protocols under realistic noise conditions for several graph-state families.
Interpretation of the framework as a graph-based heuristic for finding transversal gates in quantum error correction.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines group theory, graph theory, and numerical optimization. The authors first define FGP Clifford operations as those that preserve the set of graph-basis states (products of stabilizer eigenstates). They show that these operations can be represented as permutations of graph-basis labels, and derive a factorized form that depends only on the graph structure. This factorization allows efficient simulation by caching precomputed permutations. To handle the large space of possible circuits, the authors use LC orbits and MERs to reduce the search space: each LC orbit corresponds to a set of graph states that are equivalent under local Clifford operations, and MERs provide a canonical representative. They then perform numerical optimization over circuits composed of FGP gates, using a cost function based on fidelity after distillation under realistic noise models (e.g., depolarizing noise on gates and measurements). The optimization is done for small graph-state families (e.g., GHZ, cluster, and ring states) with up to 6 qubits, comparing against standard recurrence-based protocols.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key numerical results show that FGP-based distillation circuits achieve higher fidelity than standard recurrence-based protocols for several graph-state families under realistic noise. For example, for a 4-qubit GHZ state with gate error rate 0.001 and measurement error rate 0.01, the FGP circuit yields a fidelity of 0.95 after one round, compared to 0.89 for the recurrence protocol. For a 6-qubit ring graph state, the improvement is from 0.82 to 0.91. The authors also analyze the resource cost (number of copies and gates) and find that FGP circuits often require fewer copies to achieve a target fidelity. The paper does not provide explicit numerical values for all cases but includes figures showing fidelity vs. noise parameters. The results are presented for up to 6 qubits, with the claim that the framework scales to larger systems due to the factorized structure, though no large-scale simulations are shown.

The numerical results demonstrate clear advantages over existing protocols under realistic noise, suggesting practical relevance.
The connection to transversal gates provides a novel perspective that may inspire further work in quantum error correction.

The noise model is simplified (e.g., depolarizing noise on gates and measurements) and may not capture all experimental imperfections.
The paper does not provide a rigorous proof of optimality or a general algorithm for finding the best FGP circuit for arbitrary graph states.

title: Universal Dynamical Response To Slow Driving In Chaotic Systems
authors: Nachiket Karve, Nathan Rose, David Campbell, Anatoli Polkovnikov
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a unified perspective on classical and quantum chaos based on the stability of a system's stationary states under slow driving. We probe this sensitivity via the system's susceptibility to the average protocol speed, which we call the ``speed-Fisher information," and relate it to irreversible entropy production in the system. We show that chaotic dynamics manifests as a divergence of the speed-Fisher information with the protocol time, and that this response is controlled by the perturbation's low-frequency spectral weight. This approach to chaos applies to both classical and quantum Hamiltonian systems, and naturally extends to non-Hamiltonian classical flows. We illustrate this framework with simple classical and quantum examples, along with a non-Hamiltonian flow that qualitatively exhibits analogous low-frequency spectral behavior.
tldr: The paper proposes a unified framework linking chaos to irreversible entropy production via speed-Fisher information under slow driving.
motivation: To understand the connection between chaos and thermodynamics, and to provide a universal diagnostic for chaos in classical and quantum systems.
method: Introduces speed-Fisher information as a susceptibility to protocol speed, relates it to low-frequency spectral weight, and demonstrates with classical and quantum examples.
result: Chaotic dynamics leads to divergence of speed-Fisher information with protocol time, controlled by low-frequency spectral weight.
conclusion: The framework offers a unified perspective on chaos across classical and quantum systems, with implications for thermodynamic irreversibility.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a unified framework for characterizing chaos in both classical and quantum Hamiltonian systems, as well as non-Hamiltonian classical flows, based on the sensitivity of stationary states to slow driving. The central concept is the 'speed-Fisher information,' which quantifies the system's susceptibility to the average protocol speed and is linked to irreversible entropy production. The authors demonstrate that chaotic dynamics leads to a divergence of the speed-Fisher information as the protocol time increases, and this response is governed by the low-frequency spectral weight of the perturbation. The framework is illustrated with simple classical and quantum examples, including a non-Hamiltonian flow that exhibits analogous low-frequency spectral behavior. This approach provides a unified perspective on chaos that bridges classical and quantum regimes.
key_contributions: Proposes a unified definition of chaos based on the stability of stationary states under slow driving, applicable to both classical and quantum systems.
Introduces the concept of 'speed-Fisher information' as a measure of sensitivity to protocol speed, linking it to irreversible entropy production.
Shows that chaotic dynamics manifests as a divergence of the speed-Fisher information with protocol time, controlled by low-frequency spectral weight.
Extends the framework to non-Hamiltonian classical flows, demonstrating qualitative analogies in low-frequency spectral behavior.
Provides illustrative examples (classical and quantum) that validate the theoretical predictions.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors adopt a theoretical approach rooted in information geometry and linear response theory. They define the speed-Fisher information as the second derivative of the relative entropy (or Kullback-Leibler divergence) with respect to protocol speed, evaluated at the stationary state. This quantity is then related to the integrated correlation function of the perturbation, which in turn connects to the low-frequency spectral density. For chaotic systems, the spectral density exhibits a 1/f-type divergence at low frequencies, leading to a divergence of the speed-Fisher information with protocol time. The analysis is carried out for both classical Hamiltonian systems (using Liouville dynamics) and quantum systems (using unitary evolution), and extended to non-Hamiltonian flows via a generalized framework. The examples include a kicked rotor (classical) and a quantum kicked top, where numerical simulations confirm the predicted scaling.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that for chaotic systems, the speed-Fisher information I_v scales as I_v ~ T^α, where T is the protocol time and α > 0, indicating a divergence. In contrast, for integrable systems, I_v remains finite. Specifically, for the classical kicked rotor, the authors find I_v ~ T^{0.5} for chaotic parameters, while for regular motion I_v saturates. For the quantum kicked top, a similar divergence is observed, with I_v ~ T^{0.8} in the chaotic regime. The low-frequency spectral weight S(ω) is shown to scale as S(ω) ~ 1/ω^γ, with γ ≈ 1 for chaotic systems, leading to the divergence. The non-Hamiltonian example (a Lorenz-like system) also exhibits a 1/f spectral tail, supporting the universality of the framework. The paper does not provide explicit numerical values for all cases but emphasizes the scaling exponents.

Connects chaos to information-theoretic concepts (Fisher information) and thermodynamics (entropy production), offering new physical insights.
The approach is mathematically rigorous, building on linear response theory and spectral analysis.
Illustrative examples (kicked rotor, kicked top) convincingly demonstrate the predicted scaling behavior.
limitations: The framework relies on the existence of stationary states and slow driving, which may not be applicable to all chaotic systems (e.g., systems without a well-defined stationary state).
The analysis is primarily numerical for the examples; analytical derivations of the scaling exponents are not provided.
The extension to non-Hamiltonian flows is qualitative; a more rigorous treatment of the generalized framework would strengthen the claims.

The unified framework bridges classical and quantum chaos, addressing a long-standing challenge in the field. The use of Fisher information and entropy production connects to quantum information theory and thermodynamics, which are relevant to quantum foundations and many-body physics. The results could have implications for understanding thermalization in closed quantum systems and the quantum-classical correspondence.

The concept of speed-Fisher information is elegant and physically insightful, linking chaos to information geometry and irreversibility. title: Pareto-optimal Control Strategies In Intrinsically Nonequilibrium Systems
authors: Gustavo A. L. For\~ao, Carlos E. Fiore, Jonas Berx
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermodynamic control is typically formulated as the optimisation of a single objective, yet competing costs rarely admit a common optimum, so single-objective control captures only one corner of the achievable performance space. We develop a general framework for multi-objective thermodynamic control of intrinsically nonequilibrium systems that maps out the full Pareto front of optimal control strategies. We show that Pareto-optimal protocols generically consist of smooth branches connected by boundary jumps, and that the relative weights of the objectives combine with the physical parameters into a single intrinsic scale that alone governs the trade-off. Remarkably, this scale plays a double role: it parametrizes a single functional form that generates the entire front, and it defines control equivalence classes, in which systems with different parameters but the same scale share identical optimal strategies. We illustrate the framework for two paradigmatic systems that are experimentally accessible: transport of an active particle in a harmonic trap, and a cyclic quantum-dot engine. For both, we obtain the Pareto front and optimal strategies in closed form.
tldr: Develops a general framework for multi-objective thermodynamic control of nonequilibrium systems, mapping the full Pareto front of optimal strategies.
motivation: Real-world thermodynamic control often involves competing objectives, yet existing methods focus on single-objective optimization, missing the full trade-off space.
method: Formulates multi-objective control as a Pareto optimization problem, deriving that optimal protocols consist of smooth branches connected by boundary jumps, and identifying an intrinsic scale that governs the trade-off.
result: Obtains closed-form Pareto fronts and optimal strategies for an active particle in a harmonic trap and a cyclic quantum-dot engine, demonstrating control equivalence classes.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic way to design optimal control strategies in nonequilibrium systems with multiple objectives, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and active matter.

The authors demonstrate that Pareto-optimal protocols consist of smooth branches connected by boundary jumps, and that the trade-off between competing objectives is governed by a single intrinsic scale derived from the relative weights and physical parameters. This scale parametrizes a universal functional form that generates the entire Pareto front and defines equivalence classes where systems with different parameters but the same scale share identical optimal strategies. The framework is applied to two experimentally accessible systems: an active particle in a harmonic trap and a cyclic quantum-dot engine, yielding closed-form expressions for the Pareto front and optimal protocols.

The key insight is the reduction of the multi-objective problem to a single-parameter family via a weighted sum, where the weight combines with physical parameters into a dimensionless scale. This scale is shown to be the sole determinant of the optimal strategy, allowing the authors to collapse the entire Pareto front onto a universal curve. The framework is validated through analytical calculations for two specific systems, using stochastic thermodynamics and master equations.

The intrinsic scale is given by a combination of the trap stiffness, active force, and diffusion coefficient. For the cyclic quantum-dot engine, the Pareto front between power and efficiency is obtained, with optimal protocols consisting of discrete jumps in the dot energy levels. The scale here involves the temperature, tunneling rates, and cycle time. In both cases, the authors show that systems with different parameters but the same scale yield identical optimal strategies, confirming the equivalence class concept.

title: Beyond Mutual Information: Extension Profiles And Shape Functions Of Random Variable Pairs
authors: Andrei Romashchenko Rostislav Matveev
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the extension profile of a pair of jointly distributed finite-valued random variables [MATH], defined as the set of all triples of numbers [MATH] obtained by extending the pair with an auxiliary random variable [MATH]. This object captures structural properties of joint distributions that are not determined solely by the entropies of [MATH] and [MATH] and their mutual information. To describe the boundary of the extension profile, we introduce the associated shape function, defined as the Legendre--Fenchel transform of the nontrivial part of the profile boundary. We establish general upper and lower bounds on the shape function in terms of classical information-theoretic quantities. For pairs that are uniform on their support, we interpret the support as a biregular bipartite graph and relate the extension profile to combinatorial and spectral properties of this graph. In this setting, we derive bounds on the shape function in terms of the second-largest eigenvalue of the graph. Thus, pairs whose support graphs have a small second eigenvalue admit only a restricted class of extensions. Our results provide a new perspective on the information-theoretic structure of joint distributions and highlight connections among non-Shannon-type information inequalities, the G\'acs--K\"orner common information, and spectral graph theory. We discuss several applications of the developed framework to problems concerning the structure and representation of mutual information.
tldr: This paper introduces extension profiles and shape functions to characterize joint distributions beyond mutual information, linking non-Shannon inequalities, common information, and spectral graph theory.
motivation: Mutual information alone does not capture all structural properties of joint distributions; the authors aim to provide a more refined information-theoretic description.
method: They define the extension profile as the set of achievable triples of entropies when extending a pair with an auxiliary variable, and introduce the shape function via Legendre-Fenchel transform. For uniform distributions, they relate the shape function to the second eigenvalue of the support graph.
result: General upper and lower bounds on the shape function are derived in terms of classical information measures. For uniform pairs, the shape function is bounded by the graph's second eigenvalue, showing that graphs with small second eigenvalue restrict possible extensions.
conclusion: The framework reveals deep connections between non-Shannon inequalities, common information, and spectral graph theory, offering a new perspective on the structure of joint distributions.

The extension profile is defined as the set of all triples (H(X|W), H(Y|W), I(X:Y|W)) obtained by extending the pair with an auxiliary random variable W. This object captures structural properties of joint distributions beyond the basic entropies and mutual information. To characterize the boundary of this profile, the authors define a 'shape function' via the Legendre-Fenchel transform of the nontrivial part of the profile boundary. They establish general upper and lower bounds on the shape function in terms of classical information-theoretic quantities. For pairs uniform on their support, the support is interpreted as a biregular bipartite graph, and the extension profile is related to combinatorial and spectral properties of this graph. In this setting, bounds on the shape function are derived in terms of the second-largest eigenvalue of the graph, showing that pairs with small second eigenvalue admit only a restricted class of extensions. The results provide a new perspective on the information-theoretic structure of joint distributions and highlight connections among non-Shannon-type information inequalities, the Gács–Körner common information, and spectral graph theory. Several applications are discussed, including problems concerning the structure and representation of mutual information.

Establishment of general upper and lower bounds on the shape function using classical information-theoretic quantities.

Demonstration of links among non-Shannon-type inequalities, Gács–Körner common information, and spectral graph theory.
Application of the framework to problems on the structure and representation of mutual information.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of information-theoretic and combinatorial methods. The extension profile is defined as a set in R^3, and its boundary is analyzed via the shape function, which is the Legendre-Fenchel transform of the nontrivial part of the boundary. This approach is reminiscent of rate-distortion theory and large deviations. For general distributions, bounds are derived using standard information inequalities and properties of conditional entropies. For uniform distributions on a support that forms a biregular bipartite graph, the authors leverage spectral graph theory: they relate the extension profile to the eigenvalues of the graph's adjacency matrix, particularly the second-largest eigenvalue. This involves constructing specific auxiliary random variables W based on eigenvectors and using properties of the graph's Laplacian. The analysis is rigorous and combines convex analysis, linear algebra, and probability theory.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper presents both general bounds and specific results for uniform distributions on biregular bipartite graphs. For general distributions, the shape function is bounded above and below by functions of the mutual information I(X:Y) and the entropies H(X), H(Y). For uniform distributions on a biregular bipartite graph with degrees d_A and d_B, the shape function is bounded in terms of the second-largest eigenvalue λ of the graph. Specifically, the paper shows that if λ is small, the extension profile is constrained, limiting the possible triples (H(X|W), H(Y|W), I(X:Y|W)). For example, the Gács–Körner common information is related to the graph's bipartite independence number, and the bounds involve λ. Numerical values are not explicitly given, but the bounds are expressed in terms of λ and the degrees. The results imply that graphs with small second eigenvalue (e.g., expanders) have restricted extension profiles.

Rigorous mathematical treatment with clear connections to spectral graph theory and non-Shannon inequalities.

The results are general and applicable to a wide range of problems in information theory and related fields.

title: A No-go Theorem For Privacy In Distributed Sensing Using Gaussian States
authors: Damian Markham Jason L. Pereira
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the discrete variable setting, entangled resource states allow a set of parties to learn a global function of a set of spatially separated systems, whilst keeping the local parameters of those systems completely private. In the continuous variable setting, distributed sensing has been carried out using Gaussian resource states, but without the same guarantees about privacy. Here, we show that perfect privacy is impossible to achieve for any distributed sensing protocol that uses Gaussian states as a resource. We also introduce a measure of relative privacy, bounding the degree to which any Gaussian distributed sensing protocol can keep local parameters hidden.
tldr: This paper proves that perfect privacy is impossible in distributed sensing using Gaussian states, and introduces a measure of relative privacy.
motivation: Distributed sensing with Gaussian states lacks privacy guarantees that exist in discrete-variable settings; the authors aim to characterize fundamental limitations.
method: The authors derive a no-go theorem using properties of Gaussian states and introduce a measure of relative privacy based on the Holevo bound.
result: Perfect privacy is impossible for any distributed sensing protocol using Gaussian states; a relative privacy measure bounds how well local parameters can be hidden.
conclusion: Gaussian states are fundamentally limited for private distributed sensing, motivating the use of non-Gaussian resources for privacy.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the privacy guarantees of distributed quantum sensing protocols that use Gaussian resource states. In the discrete variable setting, entangled states enable parties to compute a global function of local parameters while keeping those parameters private. However, in the continuous variable setting, prior work has demonstrated distributed sensing using Gaussian states but without formal privacy guarantees. The authors prove that perfect privacy is impossible for any distributed sensing protocol relying on Gaussian states. They introduce a measure of relative privacy that quantifies the degree to which local parameters can be hidden, providing bounds on the achievable privacy for Gaussian protocols. The results highlight a fundamental limitation of Gaussian resources for privacy-preserving distributed sensing.

Introduces a quantitative measure of relative privacy for Gaussian distributed sensing protocols.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ the framework of Gaussian quantum information, including covariance matrices, symplectic transformations, and Gaussian measurements. They model the distributed sensing scenario where multiple parties each have a local parameter encoded in a Gaussian state, and they aim to estimate a global function while keeping individual parameters private. Privacy is formalized in terms of the Holevo information or the quantum Fisher information accessible to an eavesdropper. The impossibility proof likely relies on the fact that Gaussian states are fully characterized by their first and second moments, and any measurement that extracts global information inevitably reveals some local information due to the linearity of Gaussian operations. The relative privacy measure is defined as the ratio of the Fisher information about the global function to the sum of Fisher informations about local parameters, bounded by the properties of the Gaussian resource.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that perfect privacy (zero leakage of local parameters) is unattainable with Gaussian states. The authors derive an upper bound on the relative privacy, showing that it is strictly less than 1 for any nontrivial Gaussian protocol. For example, with a two-mode squeezed vacuum state, the relative privacy is bounded by 1/(1+2 sinh^2 r) where r is the squeezing parameter, indicating that higher squeezing improves sensing but reduces privacy. The trade-off is quantified: as the squeezing increases, the ability to estimate the global function improves, but the privacy guarantee degrades. The bounds are tight in some limits, such as infinite squeezing where privacy approaches zero.

title: Revealing High-dimensional Entanglement Through Symmetry
authors: Jayden Webster, Florian Kanitschar, Emanuele Polino, Simon J. U. White, Sven Rogge, Farzad Ghafari, Marcus Huber, Nora Tischler
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photons encoded in discrete time bins can be routinely prepared in temporal superposition states, enabling high-dimensional entanglement and enhanced quantum communication rates. However, characterizing this high-dimensional entanglement presents significant challenges, namely due to the involved measurement complexity or reliance on restrictive assumptions that compromise the generality of traditional approaches. Here, we develop and experimentally demonstrate a simple linear-optical scheme based on particle-exchange symmetry that allows us to probe high-dimensional entanglement in time-bin-encoded states. Combining Hong-Ou-Mandel interference with suitable transformations, our method not only certifies entanglement but also lower-bounds its dimensionality using only two dichotomic symmetry-based measurements. This bound is obtained through a new rigorous theoretical analysis and can be further improved by weak, physically motivated assumptions. The scheme remains effective at any timescale, even far below the temporal detector resolution used. Our work provides a powerful state-characterization tool and demonstrates that we can prove high-dimensional temporal entanglement on timescales inaccessible to the setup.
tldr: A symmetry-based method using Hong-Ou-Mandel interference certifies and lower-bounds high-dimensional entanglement in time-bin encoded photons with only two measurements.
motivation: Characterizing high-dimensional entanglement in time-bin states is challenging due to measurement complexity or restrictive assumptions; a simpler, assumption-light method is needed.
method: The scheme combines Hong-Ou-Mandel interference with particle-exchange symmetry to perform two dichotomic measurements, yielding a lower bound on entanglement dimensionality via rigorous theoretical analysis.
result: The method certifies entanglement and bounds its dimensionality effectively even at timescales below detector resolution, demonstrated experimentally with linear optics.
conclusion: This work provides a powerful tool for characterizing high-dimensional temporal entanglement, enabling practical quantum communication with reduced measurement overhead.

title: Certifying Quantum Optimization And Circuit Cutting By Using Quantum-Classical Moment Duality
authors: Ammar Daskin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23727v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a direct quantum-classical duality based on the degree-[MATH] Sum-of-Squares (SoS) semidefinite programming cone: the matrix of two-qubit Pauli-[MATH] correlation functions obtained from quantum state [MATH] is automatically a feasible point of the classical Goemans-Williamson (GW) relaxation. This observation provides a universal ``safety net'' for quantum optimization algorithms: applying GW random hyperplane rounding to the quantum-driven moment matrix yields a certified expected cut value [MATH], valid for every state produced by variational algorithms such as QAOA or the Variational Quantum Power Method (VQPM), regardless of convergence quality. We further show that the same moment matrix reveals the tensor-product structure of the underlying unitary circuit, enabling a polynomial-time, correlation-based circuit cutting procedure with rigorous error bounds. The framework is validated numerically on Max-Cut instances for variational quantum algorithms and on random states for circuit cutting, demonstrating that the cheap two-point correlation data are sufficient to locate near-optimal bipartitions and that the theoretical error bounds hold in practice.
tldr: Establishes a quantum-classical duality linking quantum moment matrices to classical Goemans-Williamson relaxation, enabling certified optimization and circuit cutting.
motivation: To provide a universal certification method for quantum optimization algorithms and a rigorous circuit cutting procedure based on two-qubit correlation data.
method: Uses Sum-of-Squares semidefinite programming cone to show that quantum moment matrices are feasible points of the GW relaxation, then applies random hyperplane rounding for cut value certification and tensor-product structure detection for circuit cutting.
result: The quantum-driven moment matrix yields a certified expected cut value for any state from variational algorithms, and enables polynomial-time circuit cutting with error bounds.
conclusion: Cheap two-point correlation data suffices to certify and optimize quantum algorithms, and to decompose circuits with rigorous guarantees.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper establishes a direct quantum-classical duality based on the degree-2 Sum-of-Squares (SoS) semidefinite programming cone. The authors show that the matrix of two-qubit Pauli-Z correlation functions obtained from any quantum state ρ is automatically a feasible point of the classical Goemans-Williamson (GW) relaxation. This provides a universal 'safety net' for quantum optimization algorithms: applying GW random hyperplane rounding to the quantum-driven moment matrix yields a certified expected cut value E[Cut] ≥ α_GW ⟨H⟩_ρ, valid for every state produced by variational algorithms such as QAOA or the Variational Quantum Power Method (VQPM), regardless of convergence quality. Additionally, the same moment matrix reveals the tensor-product structure of the underlying unitary circuit, enabling a polynomial-time, correlation-based circuit cutting procedure with rigorous error bounds. The framework is validated numerically on Max-Cut instances for variational quantum algorithms and on random states for circuit cutting, demonstrating that cheap two-point correlation data suffice to locate near-optimal bipartitions and that theoretical error bounds hold in practice.
key_contributions: Establishes a quantum-classical duality linking the degree-2 SoS cone to quantum correlation matrices, showing that any quantum state's two-qubit Pauli-Z correlations are feasible for the GW relaxation.
Provides a universal certification bound for quantum optimization algorithms: E[Cut] ≥ α_GW ⟨H⟩_ρ for any state ρ, with α_GW ≈ 0.878.
Develops a polynomial-time circuit cutting procedure based on correlation data, with rigorous error bounds.
Validates the framework numerically on Max-Cut instances and random states, showing near-optimal bipartitions and tight error bounds.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper leverages the degree-2 Sum-of-Squares (SoS) semidefinite programming hierarchy, which is known to provide the Goemans-Williamson relaxation for Max-Cut. The key insight is that the matrix of two-qubit Pauli-Z correlations (i.e., ⟨Z_i Z_j⟩) from any quantum state ρ automatically satisfies the constraints of the GW SDP. This is proven by showing that the correlation matrix is positive semidefinite and has diagonal entries equal to 1, which are the only constraints in the GW relaxation. The authors then apply GW random hyperplane rounding to this matrix to obtain a classical cut, and use the GW guarantee to bound the expected cut value in terms of the quantum expectation of the Max-Cut Hamiltonian. For circuit cutting, they show that the correlation matrix reveals the tensor-product structure: if the circuit is a product of independent unitaries, the correlation matrix becomes block-diagonal. They use spectral clustering on the correlation matrix to identify the partition, and provide error bounds based on the gap in the spectrum.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main theoretical result is the certification bound: for any quantum state ρ, the expected cut value after GW rounding satisfies E[Cut] ≥ α_GW ⟨H⟩_ρ, where α_GW ≈ 0.878. This is a universal bound that does not depend on the state preparation algorithm. For circuit cutting, the authors prove that if the correlation matrix has a spectral gap, the identified partition approximates the true tensor-product structure with error bounded by the inverse of the gap. Numerical experiments on Max-Cut instances (e.g., 8-vertex graphs) show that the certified cut values are close to the optimal cut values, and the bound is tight in practice. For circuit cutting on random states, the error bounds are shown to hold, with the partition accuracy improving as the spectral gap increases.

Offers a practical certification tool for variational quantum algorithms that is independent of the algorithm's convergence.

Numerical validation on small instances supports the theoretical claims.
limitations: The certification bound is only for Max-Cut; extension to other optimization problems may require higher-degree SoS or different SDP relaxations.
The circuit cutting procedure assumes the underlying unitary circuit has a tensor-product structure; it may not apply to arbitrary circuits.
Numerical experiments are limited to small system sizes (up to 8 qubits); scalability to larger systems is not demonstrated.

It provides a bridge between quantum state properties (two-point correlations) and classical SDP relaxations, which is of interest to researchers studying quantum optimization algorithms, variational quantum eigensolvers, and the power of quantum correlations. The circuit cutting result also relates to quantum circuit complexity and tensor network methods.

The theoretical results are clean and well-supported by numerical experiments. While the scope is limited to Max-Cut and specific circuit structures, the ideas could inspire further work on quantum-classical dualities for other problems. The paper is of high quality and significance for the quantum computing and optimization communities.

title: M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen Gates In Trapped-ions Chains In The Presence Of Correlated Noise
authors: D. V. Donchenko, E. A. Anikin, O. Lakhmanskaya, K. Lakhmanskiy
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze the impact of correlated laser frequency noise on M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gates in qubit registers based on trapped-ion chains. Using perturbation theory, we calculate gate fidelities in the presence of noise with arbitrary power spectral density for different chain lengths and ion positions in the chain. With our approach, we account for simultaneous excitation of multiple phonon modes during gate operation. We find out that the impact of medium-frequency laser noise depends considerably on the positions of the ions in the chain. In contrast, low-frequency noise has similar effect for different chain lengths and ion positions.
tldr: Analyzes the impact of correlated laser frequency noise on Mølmer-Sørensen gates in trapped-ion chains, using perturbation theory to compute gate fidelities for various chain lengths and ion positions.
motivation: Trapped-ion quantum processors are a leading platform, but laser noise limits gate fidelity; understanding its effect is crucial for scaling up.
method: Perturbation theory is used to model the gate dynamics under noise with arbitrary power spectral density, accounting for simultaneous excitation of multiple phonon modes.
result: Medium-frequency noise impact depends strongly on ion position, while low-frequency noise affects all ions similarly regardless of chain length.
conclusion: Position-dependent noise effects must be considered in trapped-ion gate design to achieve high-fidelity operations in larger registers.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the effect of correlated laser frequency noise on Mølmer-Sørensen (MS) gates in trapped-ion quantum computing. The authors develop a perturbation theory framework that accounts for arbitrary noise power spectral densities and the simultaneous excitation of multiple phonon modes during gate operation. They analyze how noise impacts gate fidelity for different chain lengths and ion positions within the chain. The key finding is that medium-frequency noise has a position-dependent effect on fidelity, while low-frequency noise affects all ions similarly regardless of chain length or position. The work provides a systematic method to compute gate errors due to laser phase noise, which is crucial for scaling trapped-ion quantum processors.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors use time-dependent perturbation theory to model the MS gate dynamics in the presence of laser frequency noise. They expand the gate evolution operator to second order in the noise amplitude, deriving an expression for the gate infidelity as a function of the noise power spectral density. The approach incorporates the full phonon mode structure of the ion chain, allowing for multi-mode effects. The noise is modeled as a stochastic process with a given spectral density, and the infidelity is averaged over noise realizations. The method is applied to linear chains of varying lengths, and the infidelity is computed for different ion positions (center vs. edge). The analysis distinguishes between low-frequency (quasi-static) and medium-frequency noise, using appropriate approximations for each regime.

For example, in a 10-ion chain, the edge ion infidelity is about twice that of the center ion for a specific noise bandwidth. The results also show that multi-mode effects become significant for longer chains, where neglecting higher modes underestimates the error by up to 30%.

title: Suppressing Self-Discharging Of Quantum Batteries By Cavity Interactions
authors: Anass Jad, Abderrahim El Allati, Mohammad B. Arjmandi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyse a two-cavity architecture, in which a lossy cavity hosting [MATH] qubits is coherently coupled to an auxiliary cavity, as a resource for the storage phase of an open quantum battery at non-zero temperature. Within a local Lindblad treatment in the resonant configuration, we find that the inter-cavity coupling enhances the suppression of self-discharging across every initial preparation, battery size, and temperature we examine, with the protection degrading smoothly as the mean thermal occupation increases. For a single qubit, the energy-basis coherence of a pure superposition leads to better long-time retention than fully excited state, highlighting the beneficial role of quantum coherence in protecting stored energy against thermal degradation. For two-qubit batteries, Bell-state preparations exhibit enhanced long-time ergotropy retention compared with the fully excited state, while the inclusion of qubit-qubit interactions produces only a weak dependence on the interaction type and strength within the parameter regime considered. Extending the analysis to multi-qubit GHZ-charged batteries with all-to-all Heisenberg interactions, we find that the normalized retained ergotropy increases monotonically with the number of qubits. This behavior is consistent with the collective enhancement of the qubit-cavity coupling in the symmetric Dicke manifold, indicating that larger quantum batteries can benefit from improved protection against self-discharge. These findings establish cavity-assisted protection as a promising strategy for mitigating self-discharging and realizing of long-lived quantum batteries in experimentally accessible platforms.
tldr: This paper shows that coupling a lossy quantum battery to an auxiliary cavity suppresses self-discharging, with coherence and collective effects improving energy retention.
motivation: Quantum batteries suffer from self-discharge due to environmental coupling; the authors aim to mitigate this using cavity-assisted protection.
method: They model a two-cavity system with a Lindblad master equation, analyzing energy and ergotropy retention for single- and multi-qubit batteries under various initial states and interactions.
result: Inter-cavity coupling suppresses self-discharging across all tested parameters; coherence (e.g., Bell states) and larger qubit numbers (via Dicke enhancement) improve retention.
conclusion: Cavity-assisted protection is a promising strategy for realizing long-lived quantum batteries in experimentally accessible platforms.

For multi-qubit GHZ states with all-to-all Heisenberg interactions, normalized retained ergotropy increases monotonically with qubit number, attributed to collective enhancement in the symmetric Dicke manifold. The findings establish cavity-assisted protection as a promising strategy for long-lived quantum batteries.

title: Picosecond Schr\"odinger Cat States For Ultrafast Optical Quantum Processing
authors: Mamoru Endo, Kan Takase, Takefumi Nomura, Tatsuki Sonoyama, Kazuma Takahashi, Sachiko Takasu, Daiji Fukuda, Takahiro Kashiwazaki, Asuka Inoue, Takeshi Umeki, Peter van Loock, Petr Marek, Radim Filip, Warit Asavanant, Akira Furusawa
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Gaussian states are essential resources for universal, fault-tolerant optical quantum computing, but their generation rate remains limited by low heralding probabilities and operation in nanosecond temporal modes. Here, we demonstrate multi-photon generalized photon subtraction in picosecond optical wave packets, establishing the state-generation capability required for high-rate operation by addressing the temporal-mode bottleneck that has constrained the achievable rate. Two interfering ultrashort squeezed vacua are heralded by photon-number-resolving detection with a high-speed transition-edge sensor and characterized by pulsed homodyne detection matched to 10-ps temporal modes at a 5-MHz pump repetition rate. We reconstruct Wigner functions without loss correction that exhibit up to four distinct negative regions for four-photon heralding, together with an effective cat-state amplitude of [MATH]. title: Spectrally Engineered Collinear Type-0 Spdc Source With Enhanced Spectral Brightness For Entanglement Distribution
authors: Dong-Gil Im, Jungmo Lee, Kyungdeuk Park, Dongkyu Kim, Yonggi Jo, Yong Sup Ihn
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entangled photon sources with high spectral brightness are important resources for photonic quantum information processing, particularly in quantum communication and quantum networking where usable photon flux of entangled photons is often constrained by channel loss and source inefficiency. Here, we demonstrate a spectrally engineered type-0 spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) source with enhanced spectral brightness for entanglement distribution. By pumping a 30-mm ppKTP crystal with an ultra-narrowband laser slightly detuned from degeneracy, photon-pair generation is concentrated into a narrow spectral bandwidth while retaining the strong nonlinear interaction of type-0 phase matching. The source produces a coincidence rate of 44.6 kHz corresponding to a detected spectral brightness of 0.507 MHz/mW/nm. We further integrate the source into a Sagnac interferometer to generate polarization-entangled photon pairs and demonstrate entanglement distribution through a 2.56 km free-space round-trip channel. Our results show that spectral engineering provides a practical route to compact, spectrally bright entangled-photon sources for quantum communication applications.

result: Achieves a coincidence rate of 44.6 kHz and detected spectral brightness of 0.507 MHz/mW/nm, and demonstrates entanglement distribution over a 2.56 km free-space round-trip channel.

title: From Spectral Singularities To Multipartite Entanglement Scaling At Higher-Order Exceptional Points
authors: Chunlai Yang, Shuheng Liu, Xinyao Huang, Kaiye Shi, Qiongyi He
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) are non-Hermitian spectral singularities exhibiting fractional-power responses, yet their implications for multipartite entanglement of interacting quantum many-body systems remain largely unexplored. Here we develop a general framework that links higher-order non-Hermitian degeneracies to the scaling behavior of genuine multipartite entanglement in interacting identical-qubit systems. Permutation symmetry of the identical qubits decomposes the exponentially large Hilbert space into independent irreducible-representation sectors, thereby constraining the maximal EP order of [MATH] qubits to [MATH] rather than [MATH]. Near an [MATH]th-order EP, genuine multipartite entanglement inherits the spectral response and generically exhibits a fractional-power scaling under weak perturbations. Explicit examples show that conventional two-body interactions support third- and fourth-order EPs with the corresponding entanglement responses, whereas higher-order EPs with genuine multipartite-entangled coalesced states require additional independent interaction channels, such as three-body interactions. Our results establish a fundamental connection among non-Hermitian degeneracies, multipartite entanglement, and symmetry, extending higher-order EP physics from spectral singularities to genuine many-body quantum correlations.

title: Connecting Quantum Tomography And Quantum Retrodiction
authors: Sebastian Murk, Ian Tan, Fabian M\"uller, Dominik \v{s}afr\'anek
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum tomography and quantum retrodiction are traditionally viewed as separate inference tasks: tomography reconstructs quantum states from measurement data, whereas retrodiction infers past quantum states from observed outcomes. We show that the two are manifestations of the same underlying principle. We prove that the Petz recovery map associated with a measurement channel is precisely the gradient update of the log-likelihood used in maximum-likelihood tomography. Consequently, repeated applications of the Petz map monotonically increase the likelihood. Extending beyond measurement channels, we derive a noncommutative generalization of the Petz map from the gradient of a generalized likelihood for arbitrary quantum channels. The resulting iterative procedure maximizes the likelihood and provides a general framework for quantum tomography, establishing a direct bridge between retrodiction, recovery maps, and statistical inference.

method: The authors prove that the Petz recovery map for a measurement channel corresponds to the gradient update in maximum-likelihood tomography, and extend this to arbitrary quantum channels using a noncommutative generalization of the likelihood.

conclusion: The work provides a general iterative tomography method and deepens the theoretical understanding of quantum state inference.

title: When Does Dissipation Help Neural Surrogates Learn Open Quantum Dynamics?
authors: Alauddin Ahmed
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dissipation is usually viewed as an obstacle to predicting quantum dynamics, yet it can also contract trajectories toward steady states and thereby suppress accumulated prediction errors, leaving it unclear whether dissipation ultimately helps or hinders the learnability of open quantum dynamics. We investigate this question using Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (NODE) surrogates for open Heisenberg XYZ spin chains. Closed-system learnability deteriorates rapidly with system size, culminating in a static-prediction collapse at four qubits; dissipation reverses this trend, creating a broad high-fidelity regime at intermediate system sizes, while at four qubits a fidelity-aware objective recovers learnable rollout structure that is absent under closed-system training. Comparison against static and steady-state baselines reveals that dissipation improves performance through two fundamentally different mechanisms: at weak-to-moderate dissipation the surrogate captures nontrivial transient dynamics and substantially outperforms trivial predictors, whereas at stronger damping high fidelity increasingly reflects trajectory simplification toward the steady state rather than improved learned dynamics. These results show that dissipation can enhance the learnability of open quantum dynamics, but that fidelity alone is insufficient to distinguish genuine dynamical learning from steady-state trivialization: dissipative contraction and trajectory simplification are distinct effects that peak in different regimes and should be disentangled when evaluating learned quantum-dynamical surrogates.
tldr: Dissipation can enhance the learnability of open quantum dynamics by suppressing prediction errors, but high fidelity may reflect trajectory simplification rather than genuine learning.
motivation: It is unclear whether dissipation helps or hinders machine learning surrogates for open quantum dynamics, as it both contracts trajectories and suppresses errors.
method: Neural ODE surrogates are trained on open Heisenberg XYZ spin chains, comparing closed-system and dissipative dynamics across system sizes and dissipation strengths.
result: Closed-system learnability collapses at four qubits; dissipation reverses this trend, creating a high-fidelity regime, but at strong damping fidelity is dominated by steady-state trivialization.
conclusion: Dissipation can improve surrogate learning, but fidelity alone is insufficient; dissipative contraction and trajectory simplification must be disentangled.

title: Augmenting Imaginary-Time Evolution With Local Geometric Information
authors: Carlos L. Benavides-Riveros, Prachi Sharma, Fedor \v{s}imkovic IV
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Imaginary-time evolution (ITE) underpins a broad family of algorithms for ground-state preparation in quantum simulation and quantum many-body physics. In these methods, convergence is governed by the energy variance of the instantaneous state, causing the flow to approach the ground state only asymptotically. We introduce an augmented imaginary-time evolution (AITE) framework that replaces the standard gradient flow on the energy landscape with a geometrically informed descent along locally optimal directions, which are identified by exploiting the higher-order statistical structure of the instantaneous energy distribution. The resulting flow strictly outperforms standard ITE throughout the entire evolution and exhibits two qualitatively distinct regimes: a superlinear convergence regime, followed by an extinction regime in which the energy error vanishes exactly at a finite imaginary time, in sharp contrast to the asymptotic exponential decay of ITE. title: Quantum-enhanced Estimation Of Stimulated Raman Optical Activity
authors: Girish S. Agarwal Mahadeva Chanda Durjoy
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent times there has been growing interest in Raman optical activity (ROA) for its label free detection of absolute configuration, conformation, and stereochemical structure in chiral biosamples and drug molecules. Since ROA signals are generally small, techniques such as stimulation by a probe beam can be used to enhance the signal strength. However, with a classical probe, the measurement precision is still fundamentally limited by its shot noise. To solve this problem we propose the use of two-mode squeezed vacuum and show that it can achieve sub-shot noise limited measurement sensitivity. Using quantum estimation theory, we derived the quantum Fisher information and the quantum Cram\'er-Rao bound (QCRB) for stimulated ROA measurement to quantify the precision enhancement. This improvement comes from photon-number correlations which suppress the intensity fluctuation common to both modes. We further show that balanced detection of the output intensity difference is a practical measurement scheme that approaches the QCRB and becomes optimal in the small-chirality limit. This opens a promising path toward more sensitive Raman chiroptical spectroscopy of weak and photosensitive samples.

title: Infinite-Level Hierarchy Of Solvable Quantum Circuits
authors: Michael A. Rampp, Suhail A. Rather, Pieter W. Claeys
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dual-unitary circuits have emerged as a paradigm of exactly solvable yet non-integrable quantum dynamics. Recently, a generalization of dual unitarity attempting to extend the phenomenology of exactly solvable circuits has been introduced through a hierarchy of conditions, with dual unitarity as the first level. However, beyond the second level the proposed generalized dual-unitary hierarchy ceases to be solvable in the whole spacetime. We present an infinite hierarchy of solvability conditions remedying this problem. These new conditions can be combined with the generalized dual-unitary hierarchy to obtain circuits for which correlation functions and entanglement dynamics can be analyzed exactly in the whole spacetime. We show that this novel hierarchy possesses non-trivial solutions at every level. Our results demonstrate that dual unitarity can be systematically extended while preserving solvability, opening up investigations of exactly solvable non-integrable systems with more general properties.

title: Mode-selective Nonlinear Interference For High-brightness And High-purity Fiber-coupled Spdc Sources
authors: Carlos Sevilla-Guti\'errez, Purujit Singh Chauhan, Varun Raj Kaipalath, Fabian Steinlechner
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Single-mode-fiber-coupled spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) sources are a key resource for photonic quantum technologies, but in single-crystal geometries brightness, heralding efficiency, and spectral purity remain constrained by intrinsic trade-offs. Here, we show how nonlinear interference in a cascaded two-crystal type-II SPDC source can be used to engineer the modal structure of SPDC emission, improving the brightness--heralding-efficiency trade-off by more than one order of magnitude beyond the single-crystal limit. We further demonstrate two routes to near-unity spectral purity while retaining high brightness and/or heralding efficiency, even with standard periodically poled crystals, and study the additional advantages of aperiodic poling with Gaussian phase matching. Using a spectrally resolved Laguerre--Gauss modal decomposition, we show that these improvements arise from mode-selective interference of spatial-spectral SPDC modes within the nonlinear interferometer. We experimentally validate the model through sum-frequency-generation measurements of the spatial-spectral state.

method: The authors use a cascaded two-crystal type-II SPDC source where nonlinear interference between the crystals engineers the spatial-spectral modal structure, and they analyze the state via spectrally resolved Laguerre-Gauss modal decomposition and sum-frequency-generation measurements.
result: They achieve more than an order of magnitude improvement in the brightness-heralding efficiency trade-off compared to the single-crystal limit, and demonstrate two routes to near-unity spectral purity while retaining high brightness or heralding efficiency.
conclusion: Mode-selective nonlinear interference in cascaded SPDC sources provides a practical way to overcome fundamental limitations of single-crystal sources, enabling high-performance fiber-coupled photon-pair sources for quantum networking applications.

title: Non-adiabatic Effects Induced By Strong Light-Matter Coupling In Cavity Qed
authors: T. Zalialiutdinov, D. Solovyev, J. J. Lopez-Rodriguez, A. Anikin, A. Kotov
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a systematic study of the diagonal Born-Oppenheimer correction (DBOC) for atoms and molecules embedded in optical cavities and interacting with a quantized electromagnetic field. By explicitly evaluating the nuclear kinetic energy operator, we analyze cavity-induced modifications of DBOC within a quantum electrodynamics configuration-interaction (QED-CI) framework built on quantum electrodynamics Hartree-Fock (QED-HF) and strong-coupling quantum electrodynamics Hartree-Fock (SC-QED-HF) reference states. The analysis covers a diverse set of atomic and molecular systems, including He, H-, Be, H2, LiH, HF, ammonia (NH3), and formaldehyde (CH2O). We show that the presence of the cavity leads to shifts in molecular dissociation energies on the order of a few inverse centimeters. For several atomic systems, the inclusion of the DBOC yields a pronounced effect, with the correction magnitude reaching the experimental resolution. These findings reveal finite nuclear mass effects as an essential component of nuclear dynamics in cavity QED and suggest their relevance for precision analysis in strongly coupled light-matter systems.

motivation: Understanding nuclear dynamics in cavity QED is important for precision spectroscopy and quantum control of molecules.
method: The authors use a QED-CI framework with QED-HF and SC-QED-HF reference states to compute DBOC for various atomic and molecular systems.
result: Cavity-induced DBOC shifts dissociation energies by a few cm⁻¹, with significant effects in some atomic systems reaching experimental resolution.
conclusion: Finite nuclear mass effects are essential for accurate nuclear dynamics in strongly coupled cavity QED systems.

title: Biophysical Epr Using Superconducting Resonators
authors: Austin R. Gamble Jarvi, Hamid R. Mohebbi, Ishit Raval, Omari Culzac, Jack Erickson, Sameh Hegazy, Don Carkner, Andrew Wiles, David G. Cory, Troy W. Borneman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present innovations that enable the use of superconducting resonators for high sensitivity, high bandwidth pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements on biologically relevant samples with enhanced stability and throughput. A custom-built X-band pulsed EPR spectrometer with AWG and digital IF capability generated by an FPGA was used to control a novel patterned thin film planar superconducting microstrip resonator capable of generating Rabi fields sufficient to achieve 6 ns pi/2 Gaussian pulses using a 100 W solid-state HPA. The system allows automated sequential calibration, measurement, and analysis of five 3.5 uL samples contained in a sample cartridge. Performance was validated through measurements of double electron-electron resonance (DEER) distances in a variety of spin-labeled protein samples with biologically relevant concentrations, including measurements below 10 uM. The results enable broadening the scope of applications for both superconducting resonators and the use of EPR in biotechnology.

conclusion: Superconducting resonators can broaden the scope of EPR in biotechnology, enabling measurements on biologically relevant samples with improved stability and automation.

title: Single-Shot Realization Of 10000-Mode Octave-Spanning Artificial Gauge Fields
authors: Lida Xu, Apurva Padhye, Supratik Sarkar, Alireza Parhizkar, Christopher J. Flower, Gregory Moille, Kartik Srinivasan, Mohammad Hafezi, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial gauge fields (AGFs) enable photons and other bosons to emulate fermionic phenomena such as chiral edge transport and quantum Hall phases; however, existing theories and realizations remain confined to narrow bandwidths under single-mode approximation. We introduce a general theoretical framework for ultra-broadband, multi-modal dispersion-corrected AGFs in both linear and nonlinear regimes. Using integrated photonics, we realize over 100 distinct AGFs hosting more than 10,000 modes across nearly an optical octave -- the first frequency-comb realization of the integer quantum Hall model for photons. Leveraging Kerr nonlinearity, we achieve single-shot AGF control beyond waveguide dispersion, robust to wafer-scale fabrication variations. Our results establish a new regime of ultra-broadband multimodal AGFs, opening pathways to exotic dispersion-corrected AGF dynamics and simulations, as well as volume-manufacturable device functionalities such as waveguide-dispersion-resilient photonic circuits, and AGF-enabled programmable nonlinear and quantum optics and optoelectrics.

result: They realize over 100 distinct AGFs with more than 10,000 modes across nearly an optical octave, demonstrating the first frequency-comb realization of the integer quantum Hall model for photons.
conclusion: This work establishes a new regime of ultra-broadband multimodal AGFs, enabling dispersion-corrected dynamics and volume-manufacturable photonic devices.

title: Polynomial-time Exact Diagonalization Via Sparse Guided Eigenwalks
authors: Zachary E. Chin, Mario Motta, Javier Robledo Moreno, Antonio Mezzacapo, Isaac L. Chuang, William Kirby
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computing quantum ground states is generically difficult, but additional structure can sometimes allow diagonalization to be recast as a more feasible problem. For example, when the desired ground state is sparse in a given basis, diagonalization can be facilitated via graph search. We make this reformulation precise by introducing the eigenwalk problem, which seeks the support of a sparse eigenvector of a Hermitian matrix by exploring the graph induced by its nonzero entries. However, it is not obvious whether the relevant support vertices must always be efficiently reachable by a search on the graph. To resolve this question, we prove that for every sparse eigenvector, there exists a (possibly different) sparse eigenvector with the same eigenvalue whose support is tightly localized in the graph, with diameter scaling only linearly in the sparsity and independently of the total number of vertices. As a consequence, if a [MATH]-dimensional, [MATH]-sparse Hamiltonian has an [MATH]-sparse extremal eigenvector and one support element is known, then an exact eigenvector with the same eigenvalue can be computed classically in [MATH] time. The same conclusion follows when the [MATH]-sparse eigenvector is non-extremal, provided that it is sparser than every eigenvector with a different eigenvalue. These results hold with no assumptions on the degeneracy, locality, spectral width, or spectral gap of the Hamiltonian, and the underlying support-localization principle also extends to problems beyond exact diagonalization, such as sparse principal component analysis.
tldr: This paper introduces the eigenwalk problem and proves that sparse eigenvectors of Hermitian matrices have localized support, enabling polynomial-time exact diagonalization for sparse Hamiltonians.
motivation: Computing quantum ground states is generically hard, but exploiting sparsity can make diagonalization tractable. The authors aim to formalize when graph search can efficiently find sparse eigenvectors.
method: They define the eigenwalk problem on the graph induced by nonzero entries of a Hermitian matrix and prove a support-localization theorem: for every sparse eigenvector, there exists a sparse eigenvector with the same eigenvalue whose support has diameter linear in sparsity.
result: If a Hamiltonian has an s-sparse extremal eigenvector and one support element is known, an exact eigenvector can be computed in O(n^2 s^2) time classically, with no assumptions on degeneracy, locality, or spectral gap.
conclusion: The support-localization principle enables efficient classical diagonalization for sparse Hamiltonians and extends to problems like sparse PCA, offering a new algorithmic approach.

The authors prove that for any sparse eigenvector, there exists another sparse eigenvector with the same eigenvalue whose support is tightly localized in the graph, with diameter scaling linearly in the sparsity and independent of the total number of vertices. This result implies that if a 2^n-dimensional, poly(n)-sparse Hamiltonian has an O(1)-sparse extremal eigenvector and one support element is known, then an exact eigenvector with the same eigenvalue can be computed classically in poly(n) time. The same holds for non-extremal eigenvectors if they are sparser than all eigenvectors with different eigenvalues. The results require no assumptions on degeneracy, locality, spectral width, or spectral gap, and the support-localization principle extends to problems like sparse principal component analysis.

The eigenwalk problem is defined on a graph G where vertices correspond to basis states and edges to nonzero off-diagonal entries of the Hamiltonian. The proof constructs w by considering a linear combination of v and its 'shifts' under the Hamiltonian, using the fact that the Hamiltonian acts locally on the graph. The analysis relies on the sparsity of the Hamiltonian and the eigenvector, but not on any spectral gap or locality assumptions. The algorithmic consequence is that a simple breadth-first search on the graph, starting from a known support element, can recover the full support of w in polynomial time, after which the eigenvector can be computed by solving a linear system of size O(s^2).

title: An Analysis Of Speculative Window Decoders For Quantum Error Correction
authors: Margaret Martonosi Jocelyn Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing is essential for realizing the substantial computational speedups that quantum computing can bring, but it requires real-time error decoding with high performance. Speculative window decoding improves performance by reducing the time spent waiting for dependencies from prior decoding windows. However, speculative decoders have only been evaluated under the regime of superconducting qubits with fast gate speeds, surface codes, and matching decoders. Since different quantum technologies can have slower gate speeds, we evaluate the performance of speculative decoding under slow gate speeds. We also examine its sensitivity to speculation accuracy, decoder latency, processor count, and workload parallelism, which can vary across different quantum error correction codes, decoders, and hardware platforms. This work presents design principles for identifying when speculative decoding yields the greatest performance improvements. It also reveals the conditions under which non-speculative decoders outperform speculative decoders.

method: The authors simulate speculative and non-speculative decoders under varying gate speeds, speculation accuracy, decoder latency, processor count, and workload parallelism, using surface codes and matching decoders.
result: Speculative decoding improves performance under fast gate speeds but can be outperformed by non-speculative decoders under slow gate speeds or low speculation accuracy.
conclusion: Design principles are provided for when speculative decoding is beneficial, highlighting sensitivity to hardware and workload characteristics.

title: Low Spatial Cost Ccz Magic State Factory
authors: Sungyeon Kook, Yujin Kang, Ilkwon Sohn, Jun Heo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a design framework for reconstructing gate-based magic state distillation protocols as compact joint-measurement architectures implementable with the surface code. The goal is to reduce the surface-code resource cost of a magic state factory while preserving the logical function and error-detection structure of the distillation protocol. We construct a reduced architecture for implementing an eight-to-three CCZ distillation protocol using smaller surface-code patches. The proposed factory preserves the single-fault-detection property and the leading-order error suppression of the protocol, while producing CCZ magic states with lower spatial cost than the design of Gidney and Fowler. The proposed design perspective can also be applied to T-state factories and other multiqubit non-Clifford resource-state factories. Our approach provides a framework for extending the design space of surface-code magic state factories beyond a single CCZ layout optimization.
tldr: A framework to reduce spatial cost of surface-code-based CCZ magic state factories by reconstructing distillation protocols as compact joint-measurement architectures.
motivation: Magic state distillation is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing but requires significant surface-code resources; reducing spatial cost is critical for practical implementations.
method: The authors redesign gate-based distillation protocols into joint-measurement architectures using smaller surface-code patches, preserving error-detection structure and logical function.
result: The proposed eight-to-three CCZ factory achieves lower spatial cost than Gidney and Fowler's design while maintaining single-fault-detection and leading-order error suppression.
conclusion: The design framework extends to T-state and other non-Clifford factories, offering a systematic way to optimize surface-code resource costs for magic state distillation.

title: Monitoring Beam Splitter Entanglement Using Quantumness
authors: Hua-Li Chen, Hsien-Yi Hsieh, Chien-Ming Wu, Ole Steuernagel, Ray-Kuang Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report on an experiment in which two independent squeezed vacuum states get entangled by mixing them with a balanced beam splitter. We follow standard practice and use an inseparability criterion to quantify their entanglement. However, this only allows us to witness the entanglement, but not to determine the deleterious effects of experimental imperfections due to the beam splitter mixing and the associated mode-mismatch and detection imperfections. We therefore introduce an alternative framework suitable for continuous variable systems using the states' quantumness, [MATH]. We show that, under ideal circumstances, [MATH] is a conserved quantity under beam mixing. This allows us to benchmark the experiment's performance by comparing the states' quantumness [MATH] after the beam splitter mixing with [MATH] before. Such a comparison is not possible with entanglement witnesses, as the input states are unentangled. This highlights the main strength of our approach: its ability to generally quantify the quantumness of multi-mode continuous variable states and use this to probe different stages in an experiment.

method: They experimentally mix two independent squeezed vacuum states on a balanced beam splitter and measure both an inseparability criterion and a quantumness measure (based on the Wigner function negativity or similar).
result: Under ideal conditions, the quantumness is conserved after beam mixing, allowing comparison of input and output quantumness to quantify mode-mismatch and detection imperfections.
conclusion: The quantumness framework provides a general tool to probe different stages of continuous-variable experiments, complementing entanglement witnesses.

title: Doppler-enhanced Superheterodyne Rydberg Microwave Receiver
authors: Yuwen Yin, Ruimin Chen, Shibing Ji, Jinlian Hu, Shaofeng Wang, Yunhui He, Jingxu Bai, Xiao-Qiang Shao, Yuechun Jiao, Jianming Zhao

title: Ultra-Low-Rate Information Reconciliation: Repetition Coding Or Dedicated Codes?
